items.stem: What is the shape of the magnetic field around a long straight wire carrying a current?
options: There is no field around a straight wire
Straight lines parallel to the wire
Straight lines radiating out from the wire
items.answer: Concentric circles around the wire
items.markingKey: The field lines are circles centred on the wire; the right-hand grip rule gives the direction.

items.stem: Explain how reversing the current in a solenoid affects its magnetic field.
items.answer: The field reverses direction, so the poles at the ends swap; the strength is unchanged.

items.stem: Explain why a relay can use a small current to switch on a large current.
items.answer: The small current magnetises an electromagnet, which attracts an iron armature and closes separate contacts in the high-current circuit.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: electromagnet attracts armature; 1 mark: closes separate circuit.

items.stem: Electromagnet X has 50 turns and carries 1.5 A; electromagnet Y has 100 turns and carries 2.0 A. Both have identical soft-iron cores. Predict which is stronger and explain.
items.answer: Y – strength depends on turns × current (75 for X, 200 for Y).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: strength increases with turns and current; 1 mark: compares the product and concludes.

items.stem: Electromagnet X has 300 turns and carries 1.0 A; electromagnet Y has 100 turns and carries 2.0 A. Both have identical soft-iron cores. Predict which is stronger and explain.
items.answer: X – strength depends on turns × current (300 for X, 200 for Y).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: strength increases with turns and current; 1 mark: compares the product and concludes.

items.stem: A school technician is asked to store some bar magnets and soft-iron rods safely. (a) State two ways to make the electromagnet stronger. (b) Describe how to find the shape and direction of the magnetic field around the magnet.
items.answer: (a) More turns; larger current (or soft-iron core). (b) Place a plotting compass at many points and mark the needle direction; join the marks into lines from N to S.

items.stem: Which change makes an electromagnet stronger?
options: Increasing the number of turns on the coil
items.answer: Increasing the number of turns on the coil
items.markingKey: Strength increases with more turns, more current or adding a soft-iron core.

items.stem: Explain how the right-hand grip rule gives the direction of the field around a wire.
items.answer: Grip the wire with the right hand, thumb pointing in the direction of conventional current; the curled fingers show the field direction.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain how reversing the current in a solenoid affects its magnetic field. (b) Explain how the right-hand grip rule gives the direction of the field around a wire.
items.answer: (a) The field reverses direction, so the poles at the ends swap; the strength is unchanged. (b) Grip the wire with the right hand, thumb pointing in the direction of conventional current; the curled fingers show the field direction.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why a relay can use a small current to switch on a large current. (b) Explain how the right-hand grip rule gives the direction of the field around a wire.
items.answer: (a) The small current magnetises an electromagnet, which attracts an iron armature and closes separate contacts in the high-current circuit. (b) Grip the wire with the right hand, thumb pointing in the direction of conventional current; the curled fingers show the field direction.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: electromagnet attracts armature; 1 mark: closes separate circuit. (b) 1 mark each.

items.stem: Electromagnet X has 50 turns and carries 1.0 A; electromagnet Y has 300 turns and carries 2.0 A. Both have identical soft-iron cores. Predict which is stronger and explain.
items.answer: Y – strength depends on turns × current (50 for X, 600 for Y).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: strength increases with turns and current; 1 mark: compares the product and concludes.

items.stem: A school technician is asked to store some bar magnets and soft-iron rods safely. (a) Explain why the core should be made of soft iron rather than steel. (b) Explain why aluminium is not attracted.
items.answer: (a) Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily, so the magnet switches off when the current stops. (b) Aluminium is not a magnetic material; no magnetism is induced in it.

items.stem: A school technician is asked to store some bar magnets and soft-iron rods safely. (a) Explain why the core should be made of soft iron rather than steel. (b) Describe how to find the shape and direction of the magnetic field around the magnet. (c) Explain why aluminium is not attracted.
items.answer: (a) Soft iron magnetises and demagnetises easily, so the magnet switches off when the current stops. (b) Place a plotting compass at many points and mark the needle direction; join the marks into lines from N to S. (c) Aluminium is not a magnetic material; no magnetism is induced in it.

items.stem: In Fleming's left-hand rule, the second finger points in the direction of
items.answer: the conventional current
items.markingKey: First finger: Field; seCond finger: Current; thuMb: Motion (force).

items.stem: Explain why a current-carrying wire placed between the poles of a magnet experiences a force.
items.answer: The magnetic field of the current interacts with the field of the magnet; the fields combine to be stronger on one side and weaker on the other, pushing the wire.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: field around wire; 1 mark: interaction gives force.

items.stem: A beam of electrons passes through a magnetic field at right angles. Explain why its path curves.
items.answer: Moving charges are a current, so each electron feels a force at right angles to its velocity and to the field; this continually changes its direction.

items.stem: A magnetic field acts north to south across the page (left to right) and a wire carries a current into the page. Use Fleming's left-hand rule to find the direction of the force on the wire, and state what would happen if the current were reversed.
items.answer: Force acts upwards; reversing the current reverses the force.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct direction using F-field, C-current, M-motion; 1 mark: reversal.

items.stem: A magnetic field acts right to left and a wire carries a current into the page. Use Fleming's left-hand rule to find the direction of the force on the wire, and state what would happen if the current were reversed.
items.answer: Force acts downwards; reversing the current reverses the force.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct direction using F-field, C-current, M-motion; 1 mark: reversal.

items.stem: A loudspeaker contains a coil attached to a paper cone, placed in the field of a permanent magnet. (a) Explain why there is a force. (b) Explain the role of the split-ring commutator in keeping rotation continuous.
items.answer: (a) The magnetic field of the current (moving charges) interacts with the field of the magnet. (b) It reverses the current every half turn so the turning effect stays in the same direction.

items.stem: A beam of electrons enters a region of uniform magnetic field at right angles to the field. (a) Explain the role of the split-ring commutator in keeping rotation continuous. (b) Describe the effect of replacing the d.c. supply with an a.c. supply.
items.answer: (a) It reverses the current every half turn so the turning effect stays in the same direction. (b) The force reverses direction many times a second, so the object vibrates (as in a loudspeaker).

items.stem: A simple d.c. motor has a rectangular coil between the poles of two magnets, connected through a split-ring commutator. (a) Explain why there is a force. (b) State what happens if both the current and the field are reversed. (c) Describe the effect of replacing the d.c. supply with an a.c. supply.
items.answer: (a) The magnetic field of the current (moving charges) interacts with the field of the magnet. (b) The force stays in the same direction. (c) The force reverses direction many times a second, so the object vibrates (as in a loudspeaker).

items.stem: Which change reverses the direction of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field?
options: Reversing both the current and the field
items.answer: Reversing the current
items.markingKey: Reversing either the current or the field reverses the force; reversing both leaves it unchanged.

items.stem: Explain how increasing the current affects the force on a wire in a magnetic field, and why.
items.answer: The force increases (in proportion to current) because the magnetic field around the wire is stronger, so the interaction is greater.

items.stem: What is the purpose of the split-ring commutator in a d.c. motor?
options: To change a.c. into d.c. in the supply
To reverse the current in the coil every half turn
items.answer: To reverse the current in the coil every half turn
items.markingKey: Reversing the current each half turn keeps the coil turning in the same direction.

items.stem: Explain why the coil of a simple d.c. motor would not keep turning without a commutator.
items.answer: After half a turn the forces on the sides would push the coil back the other way, so it would just rock to the vertical position and stop.

items.stem: Explain why the two sides of a coil in a motor experience forces in opposite directions.
items.answer: The current flows in opposite directions in the two sides, so by Fleming’s left-hand rule the forces are opposite, giving a turning effect.

items.stem: A simple d.c. motor has a rectangular coil between the poles of two magnets, connected through a split-ring commutator. Explain the role of the split-ring commutator in keeping rotation continuous.

items.stem: A simple d.c. motor has a rectangular coil between the poles of two magnets, connected through a split-ring commutator. (a) State the rule used to predict the direction of the force and what each finger represents. (b) State what happens if both the current and the field are reversed.
items.answer: (a) Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger field, second finger current, thumb motion. (b) The force stays in the same direction.

items.stem: Jonas builds a model d.c. motor but it turns very slowly. Suggest and explain three changes that would increase its speed, and one reason why a real motor might still be less efficient than expected.
items.answer: Increase the current (larger force); add more turns (more force overall); use a stronger magnet or curved pole pieces with a soft-iron core (stronger field). Efficiency lost to friction at the brushes/axle and heating of the coil resistance.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per valid change with explanation (max 3 changes → up to 4 marks); 1 mark for efficiency loss.

items.stem: A loudspeaker contains a coil attached to a paper cone, placed in the field of a permanent magnet. (a) Explain why there is a force. (b) State the rule used to predict the direction of the force and what each finger represents. (c) State two ways to increase the size of the force.
items.answer: (a) The magnetic field of the current (moving charges) interacts with the field of the magnet. (b) Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger field, second finger current, thumb motion. (c) Increase the current; use a stronger magnet (or more turns).

items.stem: Which energy transfer happens in an electric motor?
items.answer: Electrical to kinetic

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why the two sides of a coil in a motor experience forces in opposite directions. (b) Explain why the coil of a simple d.c. motor would not keep turning without a commutator.
items.answer: (a) The current flows in opposite directions in the two sides, so by Fleming’s left-hand rule the forces are opposite, giving a turning effect. (b) After half a turn the forces on the sides would push the coil back the other way, so it would just rock to the vertical position and stop.

items.stem: A beam of electrons enters a region of uniform magnetic field at right angles to the field. Explain why there is a force.
items.answer: The magnetic field of the current (moving charges) interacts with the field of the magnet.

items.stem: A loudspeaker contains a coil attached to a paper cone, placed in the field of a permanent magnet. (a) State two ways to increase the size of the force. (b) State what happens if both the current and the field are reversed.
items.answer: (a) Increase the current; use a stronger magnet (or more turns). (b) The force stays in the same direction.

items.stem: A wire is placed between the poles of a U-shaped magnet and connected to a power supply through a switch. (a) State two ways to increase the size of the force. (b) State what happens if both the current and the field are reversed. (c) Describe the effect of replacing the d.c. supply with an a.c. supply.
items.answer: (a) Increase the current; use a stronger magnet (or more turns). (b) The force stays in the same direction. (c) The force reverses direction many times a second, so the object vibrates (as in a loudspeaker).

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the two sides of a coil in a motor experience forces in opposite directions. (b) Explain why the coil in a motor is wound on a soft-iron core.
items.answer: (a) The current flows in opposite directions in the two sides, so by Fleming’s left-hand rule the forces are opposite, giving a turning effect. (b) The iron concentrates the magnetic field, increasing the force and turning effect.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the coil in a motor is wound on a soft-iron core. (b) Explain why the coil of a simple d.c. motor would not keep turning without a commutator.
items.answer: (a) The iron concentrates the magnetic field, increasing the force and turning effect. (b) After half a turn the forces on the sides would push the coil back the other way, so it would just rock to the vertical position and stop.
